extracted.intended_audience: general readers, tech journalists, security researchers, and product managers interested in Lenovo corporate history and product/security controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria about a hardware vendor's preinstalled software, firmware practices, telemetry/feedback programs, OS compatibility, and responses to security incidents. Useful for assessing vendor behavior, product safety, and remediation actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on preinstalled software
rubrics_metrics.description: Promise to only include Lenovo software, security software, drivers, and "certain applications customarily expected by users".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preinstalled software should be limited to vendor-provided core components and only those applications users reasonably expect. Avoid bundling third-party or intrusive applications by default. (Context: Lenovo made such a promise after the Superfish incident.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid installing adware/rootkit-like components
rubrics_metrics.description: Installations like Superfish were compared to the Sony DRM rootkit scandal; the incident was described as "one of the most irresponsible mistakes an established tech company has ever made."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ship software that intercepts secure communications, installs root certificates, or otherwise compromises user security or trust. Treat adware or advertising middleware that undermines TLS/HTTPS as unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with WPBT (Windows Platform Binary Table) guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Lenovo Service Engine 'did not comply with revised guidelines for appropriate usage of WPBT.' WPBT allows executable files to be stored within UEFI firmware for execution on startup and is meant to "allow critical software to persist... specifically, anti-theft security."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only store appropriate critical/anti-theft software in firmware via WPBT and follow published WPBT guidelines. Avoid using firmware persistence for non-critical or user-facing utilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not persist non-critical software across clean OS installs
rubrics_metrics.description: WPBT feature can cause executables to persist even when the operating system has been changed or reinstalled in a 'clean' configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mechanisms that reinstall vendor software after a clean OS install unless explicitly for critical security/anti-theft functionality and with clear user consent and opt-out paths. Persistence across clean installs is an anti-pattern for non-essential software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit telemetry to minimal scope and require user consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Lenovo Service Engine 'automatically sent non-identifiable system information' and the Customer Feedback program logged usage data; further analysis found the feedback program logged only usage of some pre-installed Lenovo programs and only if the user allowed the data to be collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telemetry should be transparent, limited in scope, and opt-in where appropriate. Clearly disclose what is collected, scope (which apps/actions), and obtain explicit permission; avoid broad or surreptitious data collection that could be construed as spyware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt remediation, disclosure, and updates when vulnerabilities are found
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lenovo Service Engine was discontinued after security vulnerabilities were found; Lenovo released instructions and UEFI firmware updates to remove it. Lenovo advised users to remove the offending app (Lenovo Accelerator) when it caused a vulnerability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When security issues are discovered, vendors must promptly discontinue unsafe components (if necessary), publish clear removal instructions, issue firmware/software updates, and notify affected users. Transparent disclosure of the problem and remediation steps is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ship software that creates man-in-the-middle (MITM) vulnerabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The app 'Lenovo Accelerator' was designed to 'speed up the loading' of Lenovo applications but created a man-in-the-middle security vulnerability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance or convenience software must not intercept, decrypt, or tamper with network connections. Any technique that inserts itself into networking stacks and can be exploited as a MITM is unacceptable and must be avoided or thoroughly secured and disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure supply-chain integrity and prevent unauthorized hardware tampering
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports and testimony alleged that Lenovo laptops sold to the U.S. military had been altered with a chip on the motherboard that would record inputted data and send it back to China; Lenovo said it was unaware and could not assess the allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain rigorous hardware supply-chain controls, auditing, and provenance checks to prevent unauthorized modifications that could exfiltrate data. Have procedures to rapidly investigate, notify customers and authorities, and remediate if tampering is alleged or discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support OS compatibility and avoid deliberate blocking of alternative OS installations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports indicated some Lenovo Signature laptops 'refuse to install Linux'; later a BIOS update supported Linux installs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about OS compatibility and do not deliberately block user installation of supported alternative operating systems. If there are hardware/firmware constraints, provide clear documentation and, where feasible, firmware updates to restore compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate characterization of telemetry vs spyware in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Michael Horowitz's analysis of the Customer Feedback program found it was mostly harmless and only logging some pre-installed Lenovo program usage; he criticized other media for calling it spyware when he did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or reporting on vendor telemetry, distinguish between limited, consented usage-logging and spyware-like behavior. Avoid sensational or imprecise labels; assess scope, consent, and capabilities before classifying software as spyware.
